utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, bonjour. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. Case Number IT-03-68-T, The Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Registrar. And good morning to you. Mr. Oric, again, I would like to hear you confirm that you can receive interpretation of the proceedings in a language that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, gentlemen. I understand everything that is being interpreted to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution team, together with Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and as our case manager, Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones representing Mr. Naser Oric. And we have our legal advisor, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you, Madam Vidovic and the rest of your team. Any preliminary matter you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This morning, we have a witness, but before this witness, I would like to raise some preliminary issues if you allow me. First issue will be from Ms. Patricia Sellers when it comes to an update of a medical issue. And the second one will be raised by Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio in regard to a standby of Racine Manas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with Madam Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: This is the update to securing a doctor to interview the stroke victim. I believe we've conveyed a letter to the Defence, and I did state, I think it was two days ago, in open court that we had checked with our field offices. I just want to reiterate that Dr. Milos Stevanovic, who is a specialist in neuropsychiatry now has been confirmed and secured by one of our offices. We are still at this point, as the Defence requested, trying to go through our Sarajevo office and our Zagreb office. We would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that we will be sending another letter today with the confirmation of Dr. Stevanovic, but we would urge that we be able to take a decision so that we might move forward on our 92 bis (C) motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. Di FAZIO: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. MR. Di FAZIO: Just a very brief issue before I call the next witness, and that's the issue of Racine Manas and her continuing evidence, relating to the declarations and so on. I am very, very confident that we will not reach the end of this witness today, so there will be no need to interpose her. I understand from Madam Vidovic that cross-examination will be substantial, and I'm going to be more than one and a half hours, or slightly longer than the witness yesterday. So I just can't see that we will finish with this witness today. So I am really very confident we are not going to find ourselves short. However, if that very unlikely eventuality were to occur, and I'm confident it won't, then I would not like to call Racine Manas today. There are still a lot of problems that we still have with her declaration and her annex, and we have to still give it to the Defence. So we both have problems, I think it's fair to say, with proceeding with her today. But as I said, I really don't think it's going to arise. It wouldn't surprise me if we had this witness back here next week when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I give you the floor, Madam Vidovic, please do remember that we are not sitting on Monday and Tuesday. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, I realise that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And my hope was particularly during that very short break, you will do the exercise that I mentioned earlier, to make sure that we have all the documents that we already have properly catalogued without any duplication if possible. I know that there is. I also know that there may also be a problem with the list that we were given of the documents that Ms. Manas will be -- either you or Ms. Manas, I don't know, because it seems there is some duplication already. So please try to make the best use possible that you can of those two days. That's number one. I know I am dealing with highly professional and highly efficient teams on both sides, so I am saying it because I know that you are going to do your best. But also to make it clear that this time is not going to be wasted; it's going to be made good use of. With regard to today's witness, if we can finish with the witness today, it is much better because then we won't need to keep her here. So if you can make an effort on both sides to finish her testimony today, please do. I mean, even if necessary, by making reference to parts of her statement. In previous cases, we have gone -- resorted to this when we were a little bit tight for time. But anyway, let's start, not waste time, and then we see where we stand as we go along. And we try to intervene where necessary to try and cut it short as much as we can. Yes, Madam Vidovic. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try my best to conduct a very efficient cross-examination. The question that I would like to put concerns our future work, the work for next week and the week after that. We have on our list two more names of witnesses who are to be heard, and I would like to request to receive a list of the witnesses for the week after this as soon as possible. We just have two witnesses that we know about, and this is slowing down our preparations for an effective cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, will you look into that, please. I think that's a fair request on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, we will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So anything else? MR. Di FAZIO: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness does not enjoy any protective measures, no? MR. Di FAZIO: No, there's no application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you bring the witness in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Simic. See if it is on number 4, please. Or number 6, sorry. Good morning to you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you nodding. And before I continue, I would like you to confirm to me in the first place that you are receiving interpretation in a language which is your own, which you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I am getting a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I'm glad to hear that. You know why you are here. You are going to give evidence very shortly. And before you do so, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, something similar to and equivalent to an oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the declaration, the solemn declaration, that you will make, that you will undertake with this Tribunal is that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration is contained on a piece of paper that the gentleman sitting to your left is going to give you. Please read out that text aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat. Very briefly, what's going to happen now, Mr. Simic, is that the first gentleman to your right from the bench of the Prosecution, Mr. Di Fazio, will be putting to you a set of questions. He will then be followed by Madam Vidovic, who is appearing for the accused in this case, who is Mr. Naser Oric. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you're of Serb ethnicity, and you live in Republika Srpska in Jezestica, I believe?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And your occupation used that of stonemason. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and builder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you worked for, I think, about 27 years in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Travelling on weekends to visit your family in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, did you return to Jezestica and stay there on a more permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In 1992, you had a wife and children, I believe?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: They were living with you in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Chamber a bit about the geography of the area. Firstly, you're familiar with the village of Kravica or Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How far is that would you say from Jezestica approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Kravica and Jezestica are about 4 to 5 kilometres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how far would you say that Jezestica is from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It's about 18 kilometres from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the terrain around your village of Jezestica is hilly, wooded country. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: With a lot of farmland as well?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: People raise cattle, they have sheep, pigs there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And your particular village of Jezestica was, I think, inhabited exclusively by people of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When the Trial Chamber hears you talk of places like Kravica and Jezestica, is it the case that there is a central village that is called Kravica or Jezestica, but is surrounded by small clusters of buildings called hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just want to run some names passed you, and tell me if you know these names of places. Lipinovici, Popovici, Colakovici, Mandici, Andjici, and Buljim? Have you ever heard of those places?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are those hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As far as Jezestica is concerned, does it have its hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'll run some other names. Jecmiste, Kijevici, Djermani, Rankovici. Are you familiar with those names?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And are they hamlets surrounding Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is the village -- the main village of Jezestica situated in a depression or valley and surrounded by hills?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And are some of the hamlets that you've talked about surrounding Jezestica located not far from Jezestica, but further up the hills surrounding Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't mention Mandici. There's also Mandici. That's also a part of Jezestica as well as Magasici. I forgot about Magasici. That is also part of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that clarification. Just focus very briefly on Mandici. I think you said that that was a hamlet of Kravica. In your opinion, is it a hamlet of Kravica or is it a hamlet of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: The hamlets of Kravica are those that were mentioned before. Magasici were part of Kravica, but then became a part of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go back to the question I wanted to ask you. The hamlets of Jezestica, are some of them located further up the hills surrounding the main village of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They're all around on the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is that area known locally as Brda, B-r-d-a?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The hamlets that I mentioned before belonging to both Jezestica and Kravica are located on hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Down in the flat part of the depression or valley or whatever is the main village, you've said. Is that area known as Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the term Brda is a reference to the hills, and the term "polje" is a reference to the field or flat part of the valley. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If you stood in the centre of Jezestica village and you looked at those hamlets, Jecmiste and so on, how far away would they be?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not so far. Perhaps over the hill some two to three hundred metres away. I'm speaking about the hamlets of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about the remaining hamlets? Are any of them greater distances, the remaining hamlets of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Rankovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. How far away is Rankovici from the centre of Jezestica village approximately? It doesn't have to be exact.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps 1500 metres, 1.5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you return to Jezestica from your job as a stonemason in Belgrade in about March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was your reason for returning more permanently to Jezestica in March of that year?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Because of my house, which I had spent so many years constructing, and because of my family who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the events that were starting to unfold in the former Yugoslavia have anything to do with your decision to return on a more permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. When you returned to Jezestica in March of that year, did your village of Jezestica have a village guard of some sort?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is there a small hamlet or town -- sorry, a small hamlet or village close to Jezestica called Polja?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that's, of course, different from the area of Jezestica village that is called Polje, with an E on the end?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How far away is the village of Polja?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: From the hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It's about 3 kilometres going towards Jecmiste, Kijevici, and Djermani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is there a reading room or library in Polja?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meetings there in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber was the meeting was about, who was there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: There was a meeting of our village there, and there was a person there from our village whom we had designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Then let's go through that in a bit more detail. Who was there from your village who was designated, as you say? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Miladin Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting? What was it called for?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, the purpose was we had heard when I came back from work that Muslim forces were beginning to have patrols, so we had to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that was what the meeting was about, to decide upon whether or not to set up patrols. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who actually attended the meeting? I don't need a list of names, but I want to know what people. Was it just people from your village or people from other villages?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Only people from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Men such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How old were the men? Can you give us a range? Were there young men there, middle-aged men, old men?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: From 18 to 60 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how old were you back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I'm 52 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right, okay. That's fine. Thank you. Were there any representatives of the Bosnian Serb Army or the JNA at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there any decision taken at the meeting to inform the VRS or the JNA of your decision to form a village guard? Did you tell them about it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. We did this on our own. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whose idea it was in the first place to set up this village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was our idea, the idea of the villagers in all of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, did the meeting decide upon forming a village guard or not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the decision having been taken, was, in fact, a village guard set up?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, around our houses, everybody stood guard in front of his own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few more details about Mr. Miladin Bogdanovic. In 1992, was he an old man or a young man? Do you have any idea of his age? In 1992, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He was born in 1934. I don't know how old he was at the time, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And did he have some military experience as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. But he had served his military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want you now to tell the Trial Chamber about how the village guard worked in the initial period following the decision to form it. First of all, were the village guards armed?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: As I said in my statement, we had hunting weapons. I had my rifle, for example, because I had been a hunter for 20 years or more. So the people standing guard provided the rifles, or rather they handed them over to the people taking over when they went to rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the area that you come from, is it common for men to own rifles for the purpose of hunting?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not everyone. But those who joined the hunting society and paid their membership fees there, they were able to have hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But in the village of Jezestica, there were a number of such men?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: There were about seven of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Initially, how many weapons were there available for the village guard, these hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, we had four or five pieces of -- four or five rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber how the village guard operated in the initial part, what it would do. Would it simply stand guard at the end of the street, go up in the hills, walk around at night? Tell the Trial Chamber what it did.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: We went from my house to the neighbour's house, and then they would do the same, and we would go and rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there shifts organised?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When somebody was resting, then somebody else would go and stand guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did men ever have to hand on a weapon to another man who was taking over a shift?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there a system set up of --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sorry. Allow me to finish. Was there a system set up of observation posts?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: As I just said, we didn't have any equipment. We would just go two by two. Some people would be sleeping, and others would be standing guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that. But eventually, at some point, was there a system of observation posts strung out in the area of Jezestica, perhaps outside of the village, where men would sit and stand and observe in case of trouble?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now I understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right, good. Now tell the Trial Chamber how that system worked in the initial part -- in the initial month or so after March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: These hamlets, they had their own guards. People whose house was in Polje, we would stand guard down there. And people in the hilly part, they would stand guard there. And sometimes we would have contacts with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did these village guards have any military equipment, for example, binoculars? Radio sets? Helmets? Automatic weapons? Military boots? That sort of stuff.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there a system of trenches dug to help these people who would observe?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: We had protection. Some would pile up firewood. Some would dig something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately how much territory was being guarded by this system of observation posts, call it what you will?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: About 5 kilometres across.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it a straight line of observation posts, or was it spread out in different -- not in a straight line?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was scattered. Some were up on the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there guard posts actually in the village of Jezestica itself?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. Only around the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Which houses? Are you talking about houses in Jezestica, the village of Jezestica itself?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Both Jezestica and the hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So do I take it that there were, in fact, guard houses or guard posts -- not guard houses but guard posts around the actual village of Jezestica itself? Am I correct, or is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. Around Jezestica, in Polje, and around Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did other places that you've mentioned, some of the other hamlets like Jecmiste and Rankovici, for example, have observation posts?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's all part of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you later about events that occurred on the 8th of August of 1992. But the picture that you painted so far, that you've described so far, these observation posts, shifts, men who were carrying out the observation duties, the armament, did that remain much the same from March of 1992 until August of 1992, or did it change?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It remained much the same. It didn't change very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard of a body called the Jezestica Company or Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: While I was part of the village guards, I didn't hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how long were you a part of the village guards? For what period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: From March 1992 to March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you said before that there was no VRS or JNA representative at the meeting in Polja. Between March of 1992 and August of 1992, the 8th of August 1992, did any VRS or JNA men, officers, soldiers, anyone in the VRS or the JNA come to the village and provide any instructions or any guidance or any training to the village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything like that. Or hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever leave Jezestica for any long period of time between March and August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I went to get medicines. I went to Belgrade where I was receiving medical treatment, and I would be away for three or four days at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But no substantial period of time away from your village.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no. MR. Di FAZIO: Can the witness be shown D2, please, D1 and D2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right, I just want you to cast your eye over those documents, please. And I think you will agree that you have seen these documents -- well, let me withdraw that question. Up until you came to The Hague, had you ever seen either of those two documents? Up until you arrived in this city, this town.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Just one minor matter I would like you to do, please. Could you read out the title at the top of the page of Exhibit D1. MR. Di FAZIO: Mr. Usher, would you show the witness which document is D1 so he knows. Just read it out so the interpreters can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That being the case, I think it -- is it already? What I would like to see is the B/C/S document put on the ELMO, if he's going to read it. I want to make sure that he's reading the same document. MR. Di FAZIO: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: D1, B/C/S version, just turn your head around and look at the document and read out the title slowly so the interpreters can translate it. I just want to be clear about the title. Turn your head around, Mr. Simic, and look at the piece of paper on the machine there. And read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can read it from the monitor as well. MR. Di FAZIO: I didn't realise. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you read out the title.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: List of conscripts of the Jezestica 1 Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right, now look at the names of the people on D2. MR. Di FAZIO: Mr. Usher, I would be grateful if you would show the witness D2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've seen some of those names before, I think. You've seen them yesterday when I showed you the document.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay, good. So without wasting time, are they all people from your village?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I know some of them, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can I take you to a few. And I want to ask you about their age, number 4 on the list, Vojislav Brezancic, about how old is he?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Now he is 63 or 64. I don't know how old he was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps if you can tell us the age now. Number 10, Nikola Miladinovic, how old is he?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: He was born in 1934.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 17, Dusan Ostojic, how old would he be?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I think now he's 52 or 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Number 20, Bosko Rankovic, about how old would he be?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Bosko Rankovic is now 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Dragoslav Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Dragoslav Rankovic is maybe 35 or 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So he was quite a young man back then, back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly when he was born, but this is an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Dragoslav Rankovic and Ratko Rankovic, about how old are they?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: They might have been 20 or 22 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And Desimir Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: He was born in 1934.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are there any other men that you can see in that list who would have been in their 50s or 60s back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Nikola, Desimir and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What number was that, sorry? Don't worry about answering that question. I'll withdraw the question. We'll move on. The last name at the bottom of that list, Dragan Nikolic, do you know -- do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, just forget about the list momentarily. During the time that the village guard was operating, between March of 1992 and August of 1992, did it have any sort of head or commander or leader?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did Mr. Miladin Bogdanovic play a quite active role in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: He was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he wounded in --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was he wounded in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he ever the commander or head or leader of the village guard that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: What do I know? He was a kind of leader, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: Actually, Mr. Usher, I've finished with those documents, I think, for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any notice that you were to be conscripted?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I received a call-up note. It said Mr. Simic, Miladin, and it was in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber about this call-up notice. First of all, was it handwritten or typed?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was handwritten with a ballpoint pen. There was no stamp on it or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember who gave you this piece of paper with handwriting on it that served as your conscription note?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was Miladin Bogdanovic who handed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did it have any letterhead, any official writing at the top of this piece of paper? Anything showing that, for instance, it was from the government or the VRS or Ministry of the Interior or Ministry of Defence or anything like that? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. It was just a plain piece of paper. I kept it until recently, and then I threw it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it signed by anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, could you please ask him whether he ever showed it to any members of the Office of the Prosecution before he destroyed it. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I think you heard His Honour's question. Did you ever show it to any investigators from this -- from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not before I was questioned by the investigators. This happened before. I threw it away much before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did investigators -- let me rephrase that question. Let me ask you this: Up until you arrived at The Hague, had you ever been asked about this conscription issue by anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor? Up until you arrived here, had anyone ever raised this topic of the conscription note with you from this office?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. You mean, when I got here?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not talking about when you got here. But up until you arrived here, until you arrived --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So is it the case that you were first asked about the issue of conscription when you arrived here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive, other than that piece of paper, any other document of any description at all relating to conscription?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, did you ever seek to release yourself from whatever conscription duty you may have perceived yourself to be under, you may have thought you were under? Did you ever try to get out of it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked to be released, but they didn't allow me to do that, and they said that the village guard would burn my house down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who asked -- who did you ask to be released? To whom did you direct this request?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: To Miladin Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever attend in front of any military commission or military body over this issue?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I was sent the summons from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was there -- excuse me. Was there some sort of panel or military representative who dealt with your request?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: There was one representative, a uniformed person. I don't know. I think he was a warrant officer or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were there other people there, wounded people and other people who didn't want to perform military duties also seeking to be released?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what year did you go to this commission and seek to be released from these conscription duties?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: In March 1993, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It's okay. Did you ever receive any salary, any money for being a village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't get a list or anything because I worked for a company in Belgrade, and this company would send me my salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Forget about the company in Belgrade. I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking you about your duties as a village guard. Did you ever get any money, did anyone pay you any money for carrying out your duties as a village guard in 1992 or the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I never was given any list, nor did I receive any money.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about your fellow members of the village guard, the men who patrolled and stood on the observation posts and so on? Were you aware of them ever receiving any salary? Did you ever see any such thing?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that. Maybe they did receive something, but I really cannot say because I didn't see them receiving anything. MR. Di FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be shown D7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just cast your eye over that document. The first question is: Before you arrived in The Hague, had you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you have the B/C/S version in front of you? He does, okay.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. I'll withdraw that. I want you to look very briefly at the part of the document that deals with the list of military conscripts of the Jezestica 2nd Company. MR. Di FAZIO: Your Honours will find that on page 10 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you find that in the document? Just go through the document until you find the part that deals with the list of military conscripts of the Jezestica 2nd Company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To help him, you could -- also the usher, 01320334. MR. Di FAZIO: Is it? That was exactly my problem, Your Honour. I'm grateful. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If you could, Mr. Usher, go to that page marked ending in ERN number 334. You see your name there, Miladin Simic, number 28. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, if you just turn the page back, you'll see that's part of a segment of the document that deals with "list of military conscripts of the Jezestica 2nd Company." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So your name appears under that list. All right. Now, to your knowledge were you ever a military conscript of the Jezestica 2nd Company? Were you aware of that or did anyone ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know, and nobody informed me about it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I've finished with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And just a very brief question, I don't need to show you the document. Is your middle name Ljubo, L-j-u-b-o?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was your father's name Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, my father's name is Gojko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. No more documents for the time being, Mr. Simic. Let's turn to the question of the armaments of the village guard. You've already told the Trial Chamber that they, some of the men in the village guard, were armed with hunting rifles. Did any of the men possess rifles called an M48?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: There were three or four rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that an automatic weapon, or does it need to be --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you have to use a bolt to fire off each shot? You can't just fire shots in quick succession?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know of a hamlet called Siljkovici, Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there ever any larger weapons or cannon or more powerful weapon than a rifle in the village of Siljkovici and -- sorry, the hamlet of Siljkovici and Rankovici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I heard about it. There was one in Siljkovici at the top of the hill, a recoilless cannon, and there was another one in Rankovici, another recoilless cannon. But I didn't see them, so I don't know what kind of a weapon that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You never laid eyes on it? You never saw it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If you never laid eyes on the actual weapons, have you ever seen a picture of the weapon you understood it to be?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a picture. I didn't see it, and I'm not able to explain to you what it's like or what it looks like. But I just know that they said that it's possible for one man to carry it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So one man can carry this whatever it is, this weapon or cannon?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We're not talking about a large, heavy piece of equipment that requires men or horses or tractors to move it? Is that so? Do you want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You don't need a horse to transport it. You can have two men, one man can carry it, and then he can rest and the other man can carry it. So it's possible for one man to carry it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Miladin Bogdanovic, to your knowledge, ever provide men from the area of Jezestica with any training in the use of this weapon, whatever it may have been?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see it or I didn't hear that there was any training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But you knew that there was some sort of weapon that wasn't a rifle in Siljkovici and Rankovici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber this: Do you have any information that it was provided by the VRS or the JNA to the villages of Jezestica and Siljkovici and Rankovici? Do you have any information where it came from -- where they came from?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't hear about it, and I didn't have anybody to find it out from about this weapon, where it came from and anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to take you now to the events of the 8th of August 1992. Just before the 8th of August 1992, and indeed on the 8th of August 1992, were there any VRS soldiers in Jezestica or any of the surrounding hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was the village guard operating as usual on the 8th of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning of March until the 8th of August, yes, it was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At about noon of that day, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have -- sorry. Did you have a rifle at home with you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what started to happen at about noon on the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was at home in the village of Jezestica in the field, in the village near my house. You could hear firing in Jecmiste, Kijevici, those hamlets, and Djermani. I went with a couple of my men with whom I was keeping watch there. We went up the hill from where you could see those hamlets, and we could see the men who were on guard up there running in front of us. They said that there was an attack. And then when we stopped, we could see that there were houses burning in those hamlets that I mentioned. And I could hear a voice, the voice of Biba Mladjenovic, Andjelko, called Biba, calling for help, for assistance that he couldn't stay because his brother Dragan was wounded. We went in the direction of Rankovici in order to try to save something. And we could see the Muslim forces burning houses in Rankovici. But we couldn't do anything there to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just hold it there. Now, first of all, the places that you've described as being attacked, are they little hamlets further up the hills around Jezestica and part of the area called Brda?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you make your way up the hill to any particular point?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was with you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: A couple of men. Should I give you their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I've forgotten a couple. But there was Radomir Djokic, Mirko Djokic, Ranko Djokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were all of you --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: And Miladin Djokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you all of you armed with weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: We had hunting rifles. One of them had an M48, but everyone else had hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Did you manage to get to the top of a hill?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And on the hill, the name is actually Brdo, we met the men who were in those hamlets where they were keeping watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So there was a group of men at the top of the hill, Serbs, I take it -- is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Who were guarding the -- on guard in the Jecmiste, Kijevici, and Djermani hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many of you managed to congregate there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: There were about 12 of us on that hill who managed to get together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From your position at the top of that hill, could you see Rankovici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's about 150 metres away as the crow flies. It's not much further than that from the place where I was to Rankovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is Rankovici itself on a hill?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. The little hamlet, the little hamlet of Rankovici, are all the houses clustered about on a little hill, at the top of a little hill?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you're on the top of a little hill, and Rankovici is on the top of a little hill, and it's about 150 metres away. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, from your position, what could you see was going on in Rankovici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: We could see people from the Muslim side during the attack in camouflage clothes entering the houses and burning the houses. Some were burning the houses, and some were -- and some were driving the cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We'll get on to the cattle later. But first of all, the burning of the houses, why do you say that they were burning the houses? What precisely did you see that make you say that the soldiers were burning the houses?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: You could see smoke. They would enter the house, then come out. Then you could see smoke and fire. Then they would enter the next house. These houses were not built of brick. They were made of wood, so they were easy to burn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you see flames as well as smoke?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, flame, too. Smoke first, and then flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there any firing of weapons in your direction from the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were firing at us, and some were setting the houses on flame.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From your position at the top of this hill, could you see any other hamlets surrounding Jezestica that were on fire?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could see that because when we came out, Kijevici, Djermani, and Jecmiste were already on fire, and they were moving towards Rankovici and setting that on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you tell me if -- I want to understand you. Are you saying that as you made your way to the top of the hill, you had already had a view of these other hamlets on fire? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, is it possible to have this particular spot where the witness is saying he, together with the others, was from where he could notice that it could be identified and indicated on a map, on a particular map? The reason is that it is our intention, as we said, to try and go on site. MR. Di FAZIO: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this would be important for us if we can identify the exact spot. I mean, the exact spot, I mean the hill on which supposedly the gentleman and his colleagues were. I don't know -- there should be some kind of very detailed map. You should have it available. MR. Di FAZIO: I certainly agree that that would be ideal. I've looked at the maps in preparation for trial, I've looked at the maps. And we tried to get as detailed a map that we could find. And some of them will be tendered into exhibits, but none of them, I think, have the sort of detail for this sort of exercise. And it would be ideal. The Prosecution can certainly make efforts to try and locate something more detailed, but it's going to be a special task and a special effort. And the maps that I'm aware of that we have here don't get to that sort of microdetail. But I agree it would be ideal. I can speak to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can ask the witness how one could from the village of Jezestica itself, how could one reach that particular spot? In other words, which direction to take? In other words, which -- how to get out of Jezestica and which direction, whether it's through the woods or whether it's a -- there is a street which could be asphalt or could not be asphalt or a pathway or whatever. At least, he will give us an indication now before being briefed again on this matter. MR. Di FAZIO: Certainly. I'll see if I can get more detail on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can have the break here, if it's convenient for you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. Di FAZIO: Certainly, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we'll reconvene at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, you may proceed. Perhaps you can ask him -- If I wanted to go to the same place where you were on that day watching what was happening on that little hill, small hill, how would I do it from your village? How can I find the right way? How would you direct me to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From my village, first you go straight, and then you go uphill. And as I said, this little hill where I was, from there it's like looking from this desk to the next desk. That was between that hill and Rankovici. It's another matter if you take the road and then go up the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will be able to identify it. One of your investigators can certainly identify it. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We didn't have much difficulty in Brdjanin when we went on the site visit to identify places. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, I'm sure there won't be any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be very important because distances, when you hear them here, I'll never forget in one of my very first -- early years of my career I was cross-examining very young girl, I asked her how far away were you? And she told me -- at that time we had converted to the metric system. But she went straight to metric. She said, for example, about 2 and a half metres, and since she was a little girl, I said could you show me here in the courtroom according to you what is the size of 2 and a half metres. And she told me I can also tell you in inches, and she gave -- so but then in reality, when you go and see with your own eyes it's different. MR. Di FAZIO: Perspective is something that is difficult to gain in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I will require your cooperation when trying to push this with the Registrar because obviously you need to concur that it is important to go on-site. MR. Di FAZIO: We'll do what we can in the meantime. But I'm sure there are limitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will. But first, the witness said about 150 metres, but the distance between him and here or this other desk is not 150 metres. So anyway, let's proceed. MR. Di FAZIO: I might just develop that issue a little bit, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Feel free. When I need to stop, I'll stop you. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Access to this point up on the hill that -- from where you were able to observe events in Rankovici, was that by way of some sort of road upon which vehicles could travel and also by pathway upon which only animals and people could walk?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: There wasn't a road to Rankovici. There was a footpath. And you could use an oxcart on that pathway, but not a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you've also told the Trial Chamber that you could see burning in the other hamlets, such as Jecmiste and Kijevici and so on. Could you see that burning from on top of the hill? I'm not talking about Rankovici, I'm talking about the other ones. Could you see that from the top of the hill or as you were making your way up the hill or both?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: From the same hill on the right-hand side are Djermani, Kijevici, and Jecmiste. On the left-hand side are Rankovici. You can see everything from the top of that little hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And could you actually see flames and fire coming from dwellings in those hill hamlets, Jecmiste, Kijevici, Djermani?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And one other name that I want to put to you while we're on hamlets is Potkonjice. Are you familiar with that name?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Below Rankovici, that's called Potkonjice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that also a hamlet of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you see flame and smoke coming from that particular hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's get back to the point at which you were on the top of the hill looking at events in Rankovici itself. You've mentioned soldiers who were in camouflage uniform. Did you see soldiers in any other type of uniform or any other colour of uniform other than camouflage? Or was it just camouflage soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: There were camouflage uniforms and other uniforms. And you could hear women weeping, women's voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the colour of the other uniforms of the soldiers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: They were like green.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The cattle in the area of Jezestica, how were they normally -- let me ask you this: Are the cattle that are kept in the Jezestica area normally tethered, tied up?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were cattle, sheep, there were pigs and other livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But the cattle, are they normally tethered with a rope or a chain so they don't run away or wander off or do what cattle do?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were tethered or they were kept in a barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On that day on the 8th of August, were cattle taken from the villages -- the hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The cattle were led off from those hamlets while the pigs were slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who led the cattle away?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, those Muslims who attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you were standing up on the hill looking at Rankovici at these events, did you see the presence of any women in company with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the women followed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, were these local Serb women or not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't think they would have been Serb women. It was an attack. When there was an attack, the women and the children fled down to Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What I'm asking you essentially is this: Did they appear to be cooperating or working with the attackers? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they appear at the same time as the attackers or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From what you could see, what was the role of the women?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: The role of the women was to carry something. I was unable to see what, but I think it was food.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they enter houses?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: First the men entered the houses, the houses. And as soon as the men came in, you could see fire and smoke. The women were around the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they gathering anything?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Probably yes, because they were there around the houses, and then I saw them carrying things. I wasn't the only one there. There were about 12 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But could you see from where you were, could you see what the women were carrying? Could you see what it was?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see what they were carrying, but I could see that they put this on their backs. I couldn't see what it was, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. How long did that activity last? Was it a matter of just a few minutes or did it last for half an hour or hours, the gathering of things and the carrying away of them by the women?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been an hour, and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Muslim soldiers eventually withdraw from the hamlets surrounding Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you able to -- sorry. MR. Di FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they withdraw the same day?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, you've described the hamlets up on the hills in the area called -- what you call Brda, and the village of Jezestica itself down in the depression or valley called Polje. Did Brda suffer the damage on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The houses and the livestock suffered damage. Not the land itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what about down in the valley or depression itself, the actual village of Jezestica, the area called Polje, did that suffer any damage by fire or torching on that day during the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, not on the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just one very minor point: At about the time the attack started, where did the women from -- the women and children from Brda go? Did they gather anywhere or congregate anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: They started going towards Bukova Glava and Jaglici. That's where they set off to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did any women go down into the Polje area, down into the village itself for safety?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So did the women, the Serb women, I mean, from Brda congregate down in just Bukova Glava and Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. What I saw was I knew they were Muslim women. As for Bukova Glava, I couldn't see where they went off. But it was in the direction of Bukova Glava and Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I think we're just misunderstanding each other. I'll try and clarify it. What I'm interested in is this: The Serb women, women and children who lived in this village called Brda, when the attack started, where did they go? The Serb women and children whose houses were up in the Brda area?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: They went down to Polja where there were houses, and they stayed there for two or three days, and then they went toward Bratunac to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. That's what I wanted to know. The attack starts. The women and children from Brda go down into the valley and congregate in the village of Jezestica. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, why after the attack didn't they go back to Brda, to their little hamlets? Why couldn't they do that? Why did they have to go off to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Where would they go back? Everything was burnt and gutted, the houses, the barns, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So they had nothing to go back to. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I now want you to tell the - in a bit more detail - Chamber, Trial Chamber of the aftermath of this attack. You had an opportunity to see the areas of Brda, look at it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there any cattle left?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I only saw the pigs that had been killed, and the rest of the livestock was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How had the pigs been killed?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Probably with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of numbers of pigs would there have been in the whole area of Brda? Are we talking a lot of pigs here? 10 or 12, 50, a hundred? I don't need precise figures, of course, but can you give the Trial Chamber some idea if we're talking about two or three pigs killed or bigger numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: What do I know? Every household had two or three pigs. Not more. Unless they had a sow that had piglets. Then they would have more pigs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did the villagers in Brda also raise and have sheep?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had sheep, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were sheep taken?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see any houses or dwellings survive in the Brda area?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to run some names past you, and I want you to tell the Trial Chamber if you know them. Dragan Mladjenovic. Andjelko Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: An older woman named Savka. Another woman named Savka Stjepanovic. Do you know them?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know Milosav Stjepanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What happened to them on the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As we all know in this indictment, Mr. Oric is charged only with crimes against property in these actions, so I would object to my learned friend seeking to elicit evidence of people dying or being killed because that's simply not part of this case, it's not part of this indictment. And it's not relevant to the charges of crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. Di FAZIO: First of all, it's all part of the res gestae of this case. You have to get the complete picture. If there are killings going on at the same time, precisely the same time as the torchings and the looting and the plunder that is going on during the course of the attack, for the Prosecution not to elicit such evidence is to create an utterly artificial picture, first of all. So it arises in that context. In addition, there's the allegation of armed conflict as well. So there are -- and it also goes to the question of the intentions of the attackers, whether they were to wreak havoc or not and how it's evidenced, whether it's evidenced purely and simply by plunder and burning and looting, or whether it's also evidenced by the murders. And one tends to support the other. So there are a number of reasons why the evidence is admissible and relevant and will assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may respond just briefly, there's a practical matter and a prejudicial matter, if I could address those two. The practical matter is that on the Defence side, in our preparations for this trial, we've actually concentrated on the charges against Oric. We haven't investigated or planned to cross-examine at great length on how people met their deaths, whether they met their deaths because they were caught in a crossfire, or they were fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not expected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So if my learned friend is going to adduce that evidence, then we're in the difficult position of do we cross-examine on it? Or do we remain silent? That's one matter. It's also a matter of the length of the trial. We know that all efforts are being made to keep the trials a proper length. This evidence if it's brought in each action-- of course people died; this was a war situation, there were bullets flying and people getting caught in the crossfire. If we're going to have to cross-examine each witness about how people died, where they were, whether they were a soldier, then the trial could get lengthened to a considerable degree. The prejudicial matter is the fact that Mr. Oric is charged with crimes against property; that is, in my submission, a lot less serious than crimes against a person, and it would be a little as if, in a domestic setting, if one were charging theft or criminal damage and then sought to show that the people had died, not even in the course of those crimes necessarily, but as background. We know there's a great deal of scrutiny on this case, and of course what will be reported is terrible crimes, people dying in these actions, and that the public will have an impression that that's what this trial is about, rather than it being a case of theft and criminal damage charged as war crimes. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, do you want me to reply to that? I can do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to, but I think we've heard enough. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision after having deliberated on this is that we allow the question with these provisos or caveats. We are allowing the question now, and maybe even later, as to whether people ended up being killed during one or more events that we will be talking about because this may be of relevance, particularly if the ethnicity of the persons who end up being killed is established. It may have relevance. It also has other relevance. We also want to make clear that, again, we remind you and the public, we are three professional Judges here. We know what the parameters of the indictment is, and we can assure you that if the Prosecution comes forward and brings evidence that on a particular occasion a hundred thousand persons were killed and your client is not charged with the killing of those hundred thousand persons, the fact that we have established that a hundred thousand persons were killed is not going to make your client's case more serious in our eyes because he is charged with what he is charged. And at no time are we going to even allow to get into our mind other considerations that are not pertinent to the real -- to the real indictment. But establishing that on the 8th of August, some persons were killed and that these persons were - I don't know - Serbs or even that there were no Muslims killed on that occasion may have its own value for the consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged for that clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But otherwise, you don't need to worry that this might confuse our minds and attribute more responsibility to your client than what he is being charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged. That's naturally our concern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. And thank you both for having raise this issue because it clears the water anyway. MR. Di FAZIO: It's going to raise itself again and again throughout the attacks, so it's best we deal with it at the outset. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, those names that I mentioned, you said that you know those people. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The lady known as Savka and Milosav Stjepanovic, were they elderly?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Savka Stjepanovic was younger, and Milosav Stjepanovic was older. He was perhaps 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Did you actually have -- lay eyes on Mr. -- the Mladjenovics, Andjelko and Dragan? Did you see them, see their bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We took them to the road where an ambulance came to take them to the hospital, or rather to the morgue in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had they been beheaded?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Andjelko's head was severed altogether. I heard, but I didn't see that Kemal, known as Kemo, took Andjelko Mladjenovic's head to Srebrenica and carried it through Srebrenica as a trophy and hung it up on the fence of the playing field in Srebrenica. As for Dragan Mladjenovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just want to ask you something about that. Kemal known as Kemo, do you know what his surname is? It doesn't matter if you don't.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I used to know it, but I've forgotten. I know he was born in 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And have you ever met him? Had you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is he of Muslim ethnicity or is he Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he live in the Srebrenica area, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. From near Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you describe these events with him taking the severed head to Srebrenica and so on. Tell the Trial Chamber on what you base that assertion. Why do you say that and what's your information for making that assertion so they can -- the trial Judges can assess it. What's it based on? Is it something you heard in the street, something you saw, heard on the radio? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I heard from the village of Cumavici, from the people there who had been occupied and held as hostages on the 7th of May 1997 -- 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter did not catch the year. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what year you were informed about this news.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: When it all ended and when we were able to meet, because I have some relatives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But when did the -- when did you hear from the hostages from Cumavici, when did you hear from them about this Kemal carrying around the severed head? When did you hear about it? Was that in 1992 or 1993?
