utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that I heard about it in 1994. Not before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All right. And the people that -- whose names I mentioned to you a short while ago, Andjelko, Dragan, Mrs. Stjepanovic and so on, those names, are they all Serbs or Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Mladjenovic is Andjelko Mladjenovic's brother, and Savka Mladjenovic is their mother. And the Stjepanovici is their neighbours. They're not related.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now I want to ask you to tell us very briefly about the events following August and before January of 1993. Following this attack on the 8th of August 1992, did the villagers -- sorry, did the women and children who lived in Jezestica and its surrounding hamlets leave? Did they go away?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they left. They lived in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did your wife and children, in fact, also do that, go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: My wife left in 1993. She left Polje definitely, and the children were in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So as far as you remember, your wife stayed with you following the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did a lot of other people leave -- leave the village?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. From all the hamlets on the hills, because they didn't have anywhere to live. So they sought shelter with their relatives, family, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about the people who didn't live in the hamlets but lived down in Jezestica village itself, in the Polje area? Did they leave and go live elsewhere, or did they mostly remain?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: They stayed, both women and men. They stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've already described to the Trial Chamber how the village guard operated. Was there any change that you can recall to the way the village guard operated after the attack on the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: The only change was -- well, they had nothing to guard up there. All the homes were burned. So they came down into the valley, and again they kept guard around the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Think about the period of time between the 8th of August 1992 and the 7th of January 1993. In that period of time, did any VRS or JNA representatives come and speak to the village guard or come and communicate with the villagers?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone. Nikolic was the only one who came, and he stayed instead of Miladin. He's from Kravica. I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What do you mean -- whoever Nikolic is, was he in the VRS? Was he there as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, he was just a regular person. I don't know whether he went and whether he was cooperating with somebody or together with somebody. I don't know. We didn't really talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the village guard receive any new weaponry, automatic weapons, uniforms, helmets, grenades, rocket launchers, pistols, any sort of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not at that time. Perhaps later in 1993. But it's not clear to me whether they did receive that or not. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. When you say "possibly in 1993," is it before the 7th of January 1993 or after the 7th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: After. After the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now I want you to turn your mind to the 7th of January 1993. Was the 7th of January 1993 the day of the Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you at home on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Obviously it was winter. Had it been snowing?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there snow on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On that day, how many women and children were in the village approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: A small number of them. Perhaps there were only about ten women Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the whole of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there a larger number of men in the village?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was the village guard system still operating?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Early in the morning, at about 5.00 in the morning, were you awake?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what happened at around that time.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Early in the morning, at about 5.00 or 5.30, you could hear shooting at the house of Bozo Radokic. After that, there was shooting all over the place. Shooting from weapons. We found ourselves --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just hold it there, and I want to get a few more details. Where's Bozo's house, Bozo Radokic's house? Is that in the actual village of Jezestica in the Polje area?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's to the left from Rankovici. If you're going from Polje upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. How far from your place, your house?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: When we take the road from my house, it's about 2 and a half kilometres away, as you go up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see any attackers?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they were coming down from Potkonjice, when they were closer to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how were these attackers dressed?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: They wore white uniforms. Some of them were in green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if you can, you may not be able to, but if you can, were most of them in white uniforms and just a few in green, or was it the other way around? Or you can't recall?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: More of them were wearing white uniforms than green uniforms. Those in white uniforms were walking ahead, in front, followed by those in green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were any of them on skis?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they have masks?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not masks, but they had camouflage paint on their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Did the firing initially come from one direction only?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: From all sides. You could hear the shooting from Bozo's house, from Radokici, and then the firing started to come from all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there any defence by the Serb men in the village, the village guard? Did they fire back, try to resist?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We also started firing, but then when we saw that it wouldn't do any good, that the circle was being tightened from all sides, we established a corridor towards Colakovici and Popovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you go about that, establishing a corridor? Did you establish -- by that I mean the Serb forces, the Serb men in the village. Did you establish a corridor, or was it just there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I'm calling it a corridor. But we actually started going up the hill first above Kajici. Then we walked along the creek. We followed the creek all the way up to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't really explain it because this is quite hilly terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber has understood. I think we have understood -- MR. Di FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- what he means. MR. Di FAZIO: I just want to establish one or two more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead. I just wanted to put your mind at rest that we do understand what he means when he says "establish the corridor." MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You're talking about people leaving through this corridor, and I'll get to that in a minute. But how long did it take from the first shots being fired to people starting to stream out or leave through this corridor? How long did that part of the battle last? Was it a matter of minutes? Hours? Can you tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It lasted a little longer. I think it lasted until 1.00 or 2.00. With the withdrawal, we had a lot of wounded. There was no transportation. There was just one person with an oxcart. And some people were helped along. Some people were guided by us. So then after a while, we managed to make it to Colakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. All I want to know is this: Obviously some time passed before the evacuation starts, but how were the attackers kept at bay? Was that the result of the village guard shooting back at them, holding them back, or is it that they, the attackers, did not press on? Just tell the Trial Chamber how you got that period of time to start to get this evacuation underway?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I set out above the house of Miladin Bogdanovic. There's a little hillock there. We had already come down. They had come down from the Rankovic hill. They had come down to Potkonjice. They were coming down into our village, into the valley, into Polje. Then Bogdanovic Miladin was wounded. I took him to the road, and I returned. My house was already set on fire. From the house of Zarko Djokic, there was firing at us, at me and two other men. Luckily, there was a slope, and at the bottom of the slope there was a little wood. So we could save ourselves. Otherwise, if that had not been the case, all three of us would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you saw your own house burning. Could you see other houses burning?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as we were coming -- or as they were coming down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So I want to be clear, are you saying that as the attackers approached Jezestica, they were burning houses behind them? Is that what you're saying, or not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is what I wanted to say. I wasn't able to actually go on because I was feeling sad because my house had burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Do you want to continue with the questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, if the witness needs a break, we'll give him a break. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you like a short break? Compose yourself? MR. Di FAZIO: I think it might be best in the circumstances, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll break for five minutes. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.47 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, are you feeling better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Di Fazio, he's all yours. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So I was asking you about burning houses, and you told about seeing your house burnt. I won't ask you about that any more. Did you see the houses of other people in the village of Jezestica burning?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know how it was that the evacuation started? Did someone decide upon that, or did it just happen spontaneously? How did it come about that people started to leave with the wounded on the oxcart and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: As soon as it became obvious that it was a large attack, there was nothing to wait for. The people started to leave together, and we all left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Most of the wounded were men?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were maybe two women also.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were the wounded on the oxcart?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the wounded and the dead remained in the school in Kravica and in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll get to Kravica in just a minute. Just remind the Trial Chamber again, how far away is Kravica from Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Kravica is about 4 to 5 kilometres from Jezestica. I'm not exactly sure how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So most of the villagers leave through this corridor or escape route. And where -- in which direction did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: We were going in the direction of Colakovici and Popovici, like I said before, and then we were going down to Drina, towards Polom and from there, the bus came and took us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you headed towards the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's the border with Serbia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The border, it's the border -- Serbia is right across the River Drina, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As you're making your way to this place of safety, did you go past Polja and the hamlet of Rajici and Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Rajici, yes. We passed there from Grabova, we went to Gajici, then we went through a hamlet called Momcilovici. Then we came to the stream. I'm not sure what the name of it is because before that, I never passed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But let me -- perhaps I just want to be a bit more specific. Did you go past the hamlet of Polja? Or did you at least go -- get to a point on your way to safety where you could see the hamlet of Polja?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were going towards the hills, towards Brda. We could not go towards Polja because towards the hills there were woods, and it was better. For our safety, it was better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All I want to know is this: On your way to safety, did you lay eyes on the hamlet of Polja? Could you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same as if you were looking from this table down to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right, okay. And was the place burning?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you see how many houses were burning in Polja?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the houses burning in Polja, the house of Savo. I don't know his last name. The house of Djordjo Djukanovic. That was the closest to me. The Djokic's house in Gajici. I saw the house of Bozo and his sons, Mila and Milan burning. The house of Nikolic, Rade, as I passed by there. I could see all of that burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And I want you to tell the Trial Chamber if as you -- if you passed by the hamlet of -- I think the name is Rajici. Did you go past a little hamlet called Rajici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not Rajici, Kajici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for correcting me. So did you go past that and could you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was that on fire?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Nothing was burning where I was passing. But further up, as I said, these houses were a little bit in front of the place where we passed through. We were going up towards the hills to go towards Colakovici and Popovici, but we had to pass through Kajici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many houses could you see on fire as you went passed Kajici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I saw about six houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you may not know this; if you don't, tell us. But do you know about how many houses there might be all together in Kajici?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But there were about 15 houses in that location that we consider to be Kajici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And on your way to safety, did you go past Kravica or Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I passed above Kravica. We were not able to take the road because it was being fired at from Siljkovici. So we couldn't go towards Kravica. We were going above Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In all the places that you described so far that you passed and you saw burning, were stables being burnt as well?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The stables were not burned then. But later, they burned the pigstys, the stables, and also the grain stores when they came by. And everything that was not looted was then later burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Tell the Trial Chamber how you know that if you didn't actually see that. How can you make that assertion?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I came to the conclusion that it was so because after January the 10th, Dragan Nikolic said we should all gather near the -- by the school in Bratunac and that we had to go and see the village of Colakovici and that we should organise some kind of guard there because Slapovici, the village of Slapovici, was on the other side of the hill as well as Polom, Zelinje, and perhaps we could maybe save that and prevent that from being set on fire from that side as well. And then we could also perhaps go and save what in our village had not been burned down yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'll come back to this very shortly. Just continuing your trek to safety, you've told us you went past Kravica and you looked down upon it. Could you see houses burning there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The village of Siljkovici, you could see that, and you could see part of Kravica, but not all of it. Siljkovici is to the left of Kravica on a hilltop, so it was visible. We were on another hill on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And you could see how houses burning. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where did you eventually make your way to? You said you got to a point where there were buses. Where was that location?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: In Polom, we went down from Colakovici downhill towards the Drina. The name of the village is Polom. And there we waited at the school in Polom and a bus came and collected us and took us off to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About how many people were gathered there from the Jezestica villages and hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, about a hundred and fifty were from the village of Jezestica. I don't know how many were from the hamlets because people came and went because when their houses burnt down, they no longer wanted to stand guard. There was nothing for them to guard any more. And there were about a hundred and fifty from the village of Jezestica and the surrounding hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now you say that two or three days later, on or about the 10th of January 1993, you had to go back to the area. Did you have an opportunity to see any of the destruction that you've described so far in places like Kravica, Siljkovici, Kajici, Polja? Were you able to see what it looked like two or three days later?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. We couldn't see because from the Muslim side, they were holding Kravica, Jezestica, and the surrounding hamlets. They held that for about a month and a half or two months. And we were not able to go back. When we were able to go back, I went straight to my house to see what condition it was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About when was that? When did you go back to your house?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But it was in late February or early May [as interpreted] or the end of March maybe. I can't remember the details. I know that for about a month and a half I was unable to go to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Whenever it was that you went back to your house -- let me withdraw that. Okay. You don't know precisely when you went back to your house, but you know it was about a month and a half that you stayed away. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We can all do our calculations. Whenever the date was, when you did go back, what did you see in Jezestica? I'm not talking about Brda. You've already told us about what happened to that in August. But now when you went back to the -- what did you see in the valley of Jezestica, in the village of Jezestica itself?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I saw gutted houses. The families of those who had been killed were collecting them. Some had lost a father or a brother. I was there helping to find the corpses. But we couldn't find the entire corpse. Some corpses were whole; some had been eaten by dogs. They were not all intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have you got any idea approximately how many people were killed during the course of the attack that you have been describing from -- and I'm talking about Jezestica now, not Kravica, but just about Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I have an idea about Jezestica. I know that five brothers were killed in twos, and the father and the son. And a mother called Vidosava or Vida, and she was the mother of those young men. I can't recall their names now. And Milosava, she was the wife of Djukanovic from Potkonjice. And there were other people killed as well. From Kajici, there was Gordan Nikolic [phoen], son of Cvijeto. And there was Mitar Nikolic who was killed as well. As far as I know, those people were killed in the village of Jezestica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were all of them villagers of Serb ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you continue to live in Jezestica after that, after your return one and a half months later?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. For two or three years, I stayed away in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you eventually go back to live there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Eventually, I did. I received some sort of donation to repair my house, and then I went back. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I would like to show the witness some photographs. They're intended eventually to be Exhibit P365. And they have been given to the Defence. They're available to be viewed on the Sanction system. And we can -- I think it might be best if we use the Sanction system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's first establish the first and the last ERN number of this bundle, please. MR. Di FAZIO: The bundle that I am talking about, if Your Honours' please, is a bundle commencing with ERN number 01087833 and ending with a photograph on the last page with the ERN number 01087865. That's the bundle of photographs that I want to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this will be P365? MR. Di FAZIO: It will eventually be P365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be a part of P365. Okay, so for the record, these photographs will eventually form part of a larger exhibit which I understand will be P365, which will be tendered at a later stage? MR. Di FAZIO: Yes. Well -- yes. Perhaps these can be marked for identification at this stage, MFI 365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They will need to as we go along. MR. Di FAZIO: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But eventually as I understand you, you will go to tender everything in one go at a later stage. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So go ahead. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, I want to show you some photographs. And on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right-hand side of each photograph is a number in red. And I'm going to ask you to follow which photograph I want you to look at by reading out the numbers. But mostly, they will be in sequence. Okay? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: These -- this photograph down there is from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, the top one, that has a number next to it, 7834, and the bottom one, that has got a number next to it, 7835. Now, do you know this building? If you're not sure, please say so. I don't want you to tell us --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I know where the bottom one comes from. I don't know the top one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Where do you think the bottom one comes from?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: The reading room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just ask him. At least to my -- to me, the bottom one is nothing else but an enlargement of the plaque that remains and that you can see in the first of these two photographs. MR. Di FAZIO: That's what I think as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. So perhaps you can put it straight. You have my authority to put a direct question to the witness. MR. Di FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Does the bottom one seem to be a detail of the top photograph? It seems to be a closer detail of the top photograph. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. The next two photos ending with 7836 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think he has really answered the other question. I still don't gather from what he said whether he knew exactly what this was, where it was. I think he needs to clear that up a little bit for us. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know where this plaque -- sorry, this wall is located that you can see in photographs number 7834 and 7835. Do you know where this place is? And I repeat, if you don't know and you're not sure, make sure that you tell the Trial Chamber. We only want to hear what you're sure about. If you don't know and you're not sure, that's not a problem. But do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the top one. But I'm sure the bottom one is the plaque on the reading room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's stop for a minute. And usher, could I ask you to escort the witness out of the courtroom for a couple of minutes because I need to discuss something between the two sides. So it has got nothing to do with you, sir. Usher, explain to him he doesn't have anything to do with him. Explain to him -- I mean, you don't know the language. You may have anticipated what I was after. I don't like this idea of showing the witness photos with what I gather to be a description of what they represent underneath. He should see the photo and nothing but the photo. MR. Di FAZIO: I understand that. I didn't hear anything from Defence counsel. I understand Your Honour's concern, and frankly -- if Your Honour takes the view that this should not happen with this information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it should happen. MR. Di FAZIO: -- then the Prosecution will immediately desist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is another way of doing it especially with Sanction. One can focus straight on the picture and enlarge it a little bit and the script will not show up. Because even I, who can understand very little from the language, know what this is about and where it is. MR. Di FAZIO: I am indebted to modern technology. Perhaps that will solve my problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it can be solved. MR. Di FAZIO: That's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I wanted, and I'm sure that I don't need to ask you whether you agree or not because this is definitely -- MR. Di FAZIO: With respect, this is a very sensible way of dealing with it. I don't know if Defence counsel has any views, but would it help for us to produce a hard copy showing just the photo and use that as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. MR. Di FAZIO: -- possibly for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Definitely. Definitely. MR. Di FAZIO: We can deal with it in that fashion if Your Honours please. And perhaps if the booklet is then taken away from him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now we have to wait until the usher comes back. Usher, you can bring the witness back into the courtroom, but this bundle we gave you, take it away from him, please. Thank you. Mr. Simic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are trying to make life a little bit easier for you because what you are seeing before were photos which were too small and you could have had difficulties in seeing exactly which places we were showing you. So what we are going to do is we are going to show you bigger photos which would help you identify the place better if you can. And we will go through them one by one and not put two of them together on the screen as you had before. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there is one other matter, Your Honour, which is I wonder if my learned friend could just indicate when these photographs were taken. It may be a matter which will go into evidence later, but I think it will assist the witness and probably assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Mr. Di Fazio, do you have that information? MR. Di FAZIO: I don't have that information right now, but I believe that if the Defence look at the statement of Dragan Jankovic, a witness in our case, that will be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was to assist the Court and the witness as well. It's not purely for our benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. MR. Di FAZIO: So I think that will solve the problem of the booklet itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. And we'll soon have to break, in seven minutes' time. So let's see this first photo without seeing the second and the third and the fourth, and let's concentrate on it. Does he also have a hard copy of it, Mr. Di Fazio, or not? MR. Di FAZIO: He does not, if Your Honours please, and it's only on the screen. Thank you. The witness is now being shown via Sanction the photograph depicted in 7834.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise that wall or not? And if you don't, say so.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I get mixed up. In Kravica, the waterworks has something like this, and then the reading room also has something similar. So I may be getting them mixed up. That's why I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you. Just tell us when you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the photo that shows up on the monitor at present and on which the witness has just made a statement is the one bears the number, the ERN number 01087834. Let's perhaps move to the next photo which contains an enlargement of the details of the plaque. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please -- I'm sorry. If the witness is unsure about the first one, I don't intend to lead any evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But maybe if you show him the second one and the script, the words on the plaque are zoomed in, it may refresh his memory. MR. Di FAZIO: Very well. Let's do that. Could the witness be shown 7835, and can we zoom in on the wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Does that help you at all?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, this is the reading room in Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Di Fazio. And the photo that the witness has been shown and the corresponding enlargement of this script refers to a photo bearing ERN number 01087835. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was that damaged -- do you know if that was damaged after the attack on the 8th of August or if it was damaged after the attack on the 7th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was damaged on the 7th of January, only this part of the plaque remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the reading room, is that where the meeting took place that you spoke of earlier where the village guard was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same reading room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: Can the witness be shown 7836.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that monument or what remains of that monument with Cyrillic script before?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the photo that appears on the monitor and which the witness has just made a statement about bears ERN number 01087836. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'd like to jump, if we could, to 7038. What about that house? Have you seen that before? And again, I remind you, only tell us if you're sure about that particular premises or house.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it belongs to Vaso Bogicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now or back then, in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was destroyed in 1993 at Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And whoever it belongs to, can you say that it's a house that is in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's in Polja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And are many of the houses in Polja of that similar design -- of similar design?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can we have 78 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. For the record, the witness has answered statement in regard to a photo that appears on the monitor and which has ERN number 01087038. I go through this process because I want to confirm for the record what you state in the beginning. Please show the witness photo number, et cetera. MR. Di FAZIO: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to the next photo. MR. Di FAZIO: Just for the transcript, if Your Honours please, line 1 of page 68, it should be 7838, not 7038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But what I have here clearly shows 0, and not 7838. So it may be the stamp which made the error. But we can correct it. We can correct it. The sequence should be 8 in any case. MR. Di FAZIO: Whatever the sequence is, I think Your Honour's correct. I see 7038. We'll leave it to the time being. It may be a typo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is. It shows 0. Next photo. MR. Di FAZIO: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: 7839, please. Do you -- that the clearest we can get it? That's not very, very clear, Mr. Simic. Do you know whose house that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's not clear, we can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a bit unclear. I can't see it very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I suggest we do is that he's shown the hard copy. We'll break now, prepare the hard copies, Mr. Di Fazio, and we will proceed with the hard copies. It's easier. We'll have a 25-minute break, resume at 5 to 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio and Madam Vidovic, for personal reasons of one of us, could we ask you to finish five minutes before the scheduled time, please. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes. Absolutely no problem from the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Instead of finishing at quarter to 2.00, we'll finish at 20 to 2.00. MR. Di FAZIO: I'm going to wrap this up very shortly now. In fact, just while we're on that very topic, unless Your Honours otherwise want me, I'm going I'm just going to just ask the witness to go to one more photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. As you see, I interfere the least possible. As much as I can. MR. Di FAZIO: Just to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your case is your case, and your case is your case. And I only interfere when I don't agree with you or when we don't agree with you. Yes, go ahead. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you. I'd like to show the witness a photograph that bears ERN number 01087849.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now Mr. Simic, do you recognise -- we've got the photographs in front of the witness, and I want to show it depicted on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't seem to have it. After 847, I have 851. I don't know about the other two Judges. MR. Di FAZIO: I have a similar difficulty. If Your Honours please, in my booklet, it's about three pages from the back. If you just go to three pages from the back, will that assist you? The last four numbers are 7849. Have you found them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. MR. Di FAZIO: In addition, if Your Honours please, the witness has not got the booklet in front of him which has got the writing so that should be taken away, so he's only got what he sees on the screen. Mr. Usher, could you remove it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, do you see that house depicted there, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: This house is perhaps Simic Miladin's house. And the house of Rajo Mladjenovic because we built it all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just to put matters simply, is it your place? Is it your house?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to your house whenever it was, about one and a half months after the attack in January, was it in this condition or was it different? Did it look differently? Or you can't recall?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was in this state. It was the same. The only thing is that the roof was burned, but you can't see that on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, did it -- you can see some Cyrillic writing above the doors. What does that say?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I cannot see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just a moment. Don't worry. There we are. Can you see that writing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well if he can see, then we are not seeing the same thing, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. Di FAZIO: I see on my screen the writing highlighted. You don't have that, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are seeing everything blank. But anyway, let's try the others. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours bear with me, it's a technical glitch. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least it's very dark. What we have is very dark. I don't know if the -- MR. Di FAZIO: I have a photograph of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show it. We have the photo, too. MR. Di FAZIO: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have a look at that photograph. Do you recognise that house? Is that yours?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you see the Cyrillic writing?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It says here "Izvidjaci," pioneers or reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And to the left is a symbol. I think that might be a Serb symbol of some sort. Do you recognise that? The four Cs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The four Cs.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see those four letters. I don't know what that means, and I don't know who wrote that. When I came back, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So this -- when you came back one and a half months after the attack in January 1993, that symbol and that writing was on your house. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Look closely at the house. It looks to me as if it has wooden frames in the doorway and in the windows.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it's just broken or smashed. That is correct. Everything that could be removed and taken away was removed and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. It's just a very simple little question. There seem to be wooden frames around the window and doors.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they burned when your house was burned or not, how is it that there were wooden frames? Is it the house was only partially burnt? That those wooden frames were always there? They were replaced? They were not the wooden frames you had on the house? That's all I'm asking. If the place was damaged by fire, how is it that the wooden frames are there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: The fire damaged all the wooden construction. When I came back, it was all destroyed and it was all blackened by the smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you came back one and a half months later after 1993, were those wooden frames in the windows and the door, were they there? Or is this photo showing something that's been added later?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was all there before. Nothing was added. On the ground floor, I still have that same window. I didn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So your position is that what you see in the front of that house, including the wooden frames and doors, were there as part of your house even before the attack on the 8th of January -- on the 7th of January 1993? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: I've finished with that. Would Your Honours just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And there's one last matter that I must ask you about. Were you ever given any compensation for any of the damage to your house or any belongings that may have been taken from your house after the attacks that you've described?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received 5.000 German marks for repairs in 1995 -- no, I'm sorry, in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because it's not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not 1995 because he corrected himself, but he can't be 2005 because although we all aspire --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I'm sorry. I apologise. I received this in 1995, 5.000 dinars for repairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That clears it up. Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know who the compensation came from? And I want you to be absolutely certain about this, no speculation. Do you know who provided you with the compensation, who gave you the 5.000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I received it from the municipality. The people from the municipality gave it to me for repairs. I don't know where they got it from. I don't know how they got this money.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: A municipality that forms part of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any compensation from the Bosnian Muslim Army or the forces associated with the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to rise to my feet. Republika Srpska is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's a very confusing question, really. I'm not sure whether my learned friend is suggesting that Republika Srpska is a separate nation or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's going to confuse anyone. Leave it. We know exactly what the situation is. I think what the -- what counsel is trying to elicit from the witness is whether in addition to any money he may have received from the Municipality of Bratunac, which forms part of Republika Srpska, whether he has also received anything else from the Bosnian Army, the -- MR. Di FAZIO: BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The BiH Army is the government army of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a very valid question whether in addition to the money he has received from Bratunac municipality, he has received anything else from elsewhere. MR. Di FAZIO: That's a very simple question. Let me repeat His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Apart from the compensation you received from the Municipality of Bratunac, have you received compensation from anywhere else, any other entity?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I just lost my health, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. Di FAZIO: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it, Madam Vidovic, you will not finish the cross-examination today. So you may start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can start, and I will try my best to be as effective as possible, or as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, in the former Yugoslavia, it was compulsory for all men of age to serve in the military. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the former Yugoslavia. I served my compulsory military duty also.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the other men of age from your village, did they also serve their compulsory military term?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did serve it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question refers to the situation as it was before the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of those who were of age, who came of age, went to serve in Serbia or in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Miladin Bogdanovic is no exception in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to something that occurs when English-speaking components of the Chamber or of the trial are conversing amongst themselves, but also when the Serbo-Croat language is being used by witness and counsel. There is a tendency not to allow an interval between question and answer and question, which creates a little -- not a little bit, a lot of problems for the interpreters. So Mr. Simic, when Madam Vidovic puts a question to you, please allow a very small, short interval of time before you start answering so that we get the translation of what she would have put to you as a question. And similarly, Madam Vidovic, after he's finished answering your question, please, let us have -- let us receive interpretation in time. I know that we do the same mistake all the time. So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I asked you, Mr. Miladin Bogdanovic was not any kind of exception regarding the serving of this compulsory military duty? He was not the only person who had served his compulsory term?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. Are you talking about the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did serve in the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just like the other citizens did.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, just like the other citizens did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did I understand you properly that you came to Jezestica regularly every week before the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you knew what was happening in the village of Jezestica and Kravica local community?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything in March 1992. But in March of 1992, I found out what was going on, and then I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am not suggesting with this question any kind of wartime events, but I'm just asking you generally whether you knew what was going on in the village of Jezestica and your local commune of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. But I had to go away to work, and then I would come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Simic, you said that you were a hunter.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That means that you knew that area very well and that you moved around a lot there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew it. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the defence in your village was established in March 1992. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it's also correct that Jezestica is part of the Kravica local commune. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, preparations for war in your village and your Kravica local commune started much earlier. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about Kravica. But I know about Jezestica. I wasn't really interested in what was going on in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness please be shown the second paragraph of page 37 of the "Bloody Christmas the village of Kravica" by author Boro Miljanovic published in 1996 in Belgrade. There is also the cover page of the book that we are enclosing. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, are there copies coming? Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The book refers to the events in Kravica that we are discussing here. I would like to quote a relevant part of page 37, Mr. Simic. Could you please look at it. "The organising of the Serbian people for defence was undertaken by the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, which at its promotion for this area on the 19th of August 1991 established with the programme that it adopted as its main focus the national interest as well as the preparation of the population for defence" and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you about things that I don't know anything about. But as far as what I know, I told you when I came back and when I started to participate in the village guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the cover page of the "Bloody Christmas of the village of Kravica" by author Boro Miljanovic be tendered as an a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be D11. No?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D11. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. Di FAZIO: -- I'm simply not following this. It's the front cover of a book. What's the relevance of it, if Your Honours please? How is this going to help you to decide the issues in the trial? I don't want to stand in the way, but I just don't quite understand how it is linked to this case and how anything that this witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know what my learned friend has in front of him. But I enclosed the cover page of the -- or the title page of the book so you could see the author of the book, exactly which book we are talking about. But I also attached page 37 in the original, and I quoted the relevant part of that book. The translation of that part of the book follows. Of course, Your Honours, I requested the whole page to be translated, but the translating service asked me that only the relevant parts that I would use be translated. So following the original page 37, there is a translation of the relevant part which I quoted. MR. Di FAZIO: Well, again, Your Honours, it's -- I don't want to be a stickler for technical detail, but all you have is the front cover of a book, one page from a book, and it says something about which this witness knows nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the fact that the witness knows nothing about it doesn't make the entry or the document irrelevant. So perhaps the answer that Madam Vidovic hasn't given us yet is what is the relevance of this excerpt from page 37 that you have questioned the witness about? That's all you need to tell us, and then we can decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does the witness know that the SDS organised a crisis staff in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that is correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If I would have known this, I would have told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would now like to ask that the witness be shown page 43 of this same book, "Bloody Christmas in the village of Kravica" by author Boro Milovanovic published in Belgrade in 1996. The first paragraph on page 43. And from my next question, you will see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you said that the lines of defence were established in your village at the start of the war. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I did not say that they were established. I said that they were established. For example man was -- or the distance between men was 1 metre. And as a village guard, we would -- the distance between one man and the next was between 10 to 15 metres. So this is not an established line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is still a line of defence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is some kind of line, but it's not fortified or established the way you are trying to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am now asking you to look at the first paragraph of page 43 of this book which states: "The staff determined the lines of defence in all settlements from Banjevici, Donja and Gornja Brana, Bacici, Jezero, Mratinjaci, Gornji and Donji Dolovi, Brezanci, Jasikovaca, Ravni Buljim Jezestica (Jaglic, Djermani, Vresinje) followed by Magasici (Mjenice, Radukici, Bozici, Deronjici) through Avdagina Njiva and Mandici to Bandijera." Are you stating that this is not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: That is correct. But I don't know who determined this, who established this. I could not tell you that. I'm not sure whether anybody did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the gist is that you claim that it is correct that this line did exist.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Everyone was protecting their own home. In all of these villages, everybody was protecting their own homes until they lost these homes. And then after that, it was all different.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Simic, this quote from the book which refers to the line of defence, regardless of who established it, is correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know who established it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm saying. Regardless of who established it.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know who established it, but as for whether we did maintain a village guard, we did maintain it. They maintained it in their hamlets, and we maintained it in ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would ask for this part of the book, the quoted part of the book on page 43, be tendered as a Defence exhibit. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the point that we've reached with this evidence is this: An author -- part of a book has been put to the witness saying X. The witness has given evidence about his own knowledge, and this is being sought to be tendered into evidence. I just don't see how it can assist you. A, it's just part of a book, of course, and you don't get the full context. Secondly, I had rather expected that what Madam Vidovic would do would be to put a proposition to the witness and say there was a line of defence established between these places, is that correct or not? The witness would give his answer. And if she didn't like the answer, she would then confront the witness with a book and say does this change your mind? Does this influence you now that you see this? Are you affected in some way? Is your answer, your evidence altered? In that particular manner. But all that we have is the witness giving his evidence and quotes from a book. It's just getting nowhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know as much as I do that cross-examination styles differ from -- depending on obviously which jurisdiction you're coming from. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we make allowances all the time. I agree with you that would have been the more correct approach. On the other hand, as regards the relevance, I am allowing these questions so far, unless I'm convinced that we shouldn't proceed along these lines, on the basis that what obviously the Defence is trying to prove is that well before the attacks, the area was already part of the strategic plan of the SDS, of the Serbian authorities, and that they had already plans for concentrating defence efforts in the area, starting way back from August 1991. So the relevance is there. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes. I have absolutely no problem with that, of course, and the Defence have to do that; it's part of their job. I've got no problem with them trying to establish that. And they have got a witness here they can ask about that. And I've got no problem with that either. But I don't see that putting in part of a book by someone saying that is something that this witness can really help you with. But I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't pursue it. I wouldn't pursue it, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. Di FAZIO: Perhaps it's a question of weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a question of -- I mean, Judge Eser wanted to put a question in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, for my own clarification with regard to language, in the English it reads "defence lines." Now, what was your proposition? Was it that there was one line drawn, or does the book talk of lines regarding -- with regard to individual villages? So I think the difference whether you had a line which is drawn along a couple of villages or whether you have lines around one or each village where you may have your own guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the book, it says "the staff established defence lines in all hamlets." So it's in the plural. Your Honours, very briefly I put a question to the witness as to who had established the defence line. And the exhibit I tendered was, in fact, something that followed from my question to the witness. I would now like to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but before you move on, we need to clear this up. I noticed that while you were reading from the original text, when you arrived at the section mentioning Jezestica and then in brackets those three hamlets, you mentioned "Jaglici, Djermani, and Vresinje," in the English translation that we have, we have "Jaglici, Burmani and Vresinje." We don't have Djermani; we have a Burmani. Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is evidently a typographical error, Your Honour. Please understand that these translations were done very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not blaming anyone, at least of all you, Madam Vidovic. I'm just raising the matter for the record, and I'm correcting my own entry. So shall we proceed or shall we stop. You have approximately four minutes. You choose whether you can cover any other territory in four minutes or whether we need to stop here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to stop here because this is a broad topic, and I will need more time to go into it. Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can be escorted out. Let me explain to you, Mr. Simic. We can't finish your testimony today. We will continue on Wednesday, also because we need to prepare other things in the meantime. You will be taken care of in the next few Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. days to make sure that your stay here in The Hague is to your satisfaction. In the meantime, rest as much as you can so that on Wednesday when we see you again you will be as fresh as you were this morning when you started giving evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First, next witness, is it going to be Ms. Manas on Wednesday after we're finished with the witness, or that other witness which you have on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The other witness on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we expect on Wednesday to finish with this witness. Madam Vidovic, do you think you would be in a position to finish with this witness on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have the other witness. I am not mentioning the name because I am not exactly aware at the moment whether she has -- but anyway. Next witness should be available on Wednesday then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it that Ms. Manas is not going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Not for the time being, but we are still keeping her standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I would also like you to use Monday and Tuesday to finish the exercise of burning the videos into CDs or DVDs. I think that process you have undertaken already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's confirmed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And make sure that my staff is provided with the necessary...

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The understanding also is that those photos that you referred to in the course of the evidence we are going to keep them here, but the document itself hasn't been tendered, P365. MR. Di FAZIO: It has just been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further points because we need to finish in two minutes? MR. Di FAZIO: Just one matter: I wasn't here yesterday, but I understand Your Honours issued some directions regarding the provision for intended exhibits by the Defence. Now, I hope I haven't got a mixed understanding here. I only just got those documents as they were coming in. I'm not complaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should complain. MR. Di FAZIO: Can't be perfect, but in future, could we have them earlier if they're available. I understand that can't always happen, but generally if it could happen in advance, that would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, very quickly, please. Madam Vidovic, you will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday I talked to Mr. Wubben, and I said clearly that we would be using documents they already have in their archives. I mentioned I would deliver a list of numbers, the numbers -- the Prosecution numbers on these documents. And we did this last night. Also, I added to this list a brief description of the exhibits which do not have Prosecution numbers. These are inserts from the Kravica. So all they had to do was take these documents out of their own archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not make an issue out of it now because we need to go. But try to cooperate. Don't try to go into confrontation on this because then we will have to step in. Thank you. Have a nice weekend, everyone. And if it please God, we will meet on Wednesday morning. I will be here Monday and Tuesday in case you have any problems amongst you that you need to discuss. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
